sections.b: At the height of his power David stays home from war, takes Bathsheba, the wife of one of his own elite soldiers, and when she becomes pregnant arranges her husband Uriah's death (2 Samuel 11). The narrator's verdict is short: what David had done looked evil in the LORD's eyes (2 Samuel 11:27). Nathan's parable traps the king into condemning himself, and David confesses without excuse (2 Samuel 12:1–13). He is forgiven, but the consequences follow: the child dies, his son Amnon rapes his daughter Tamar, Absalom murders Amnon, and Absalom drives David from Jerusalem and takes his concubines in public (2 Samuel 13–16). David's response in these chapters is often humble: he sends back the ark, accepts Shimei's curses as possibly from God, and weeps for the son who tried to kill him (2 Samuel 15:25–26; 2 Samuel 16:10–12; 2 Samuel 18:33). Many readers find in these chapters the most honest portrait of a ruler in ancient literature.

common: David's sin with Bathsheba is the turning point of his reign: after it, his family and kingdom are troubled to the end.
uncommon: Some critical historians think the Bathsheba story was preserved because it explained, and partly justified, how Solomon, a younger son, came to the throne.

claude.title: Claude's reading: from sending to releasing
claude.body: My own reading: in 2 Samuel 11 David "sends" again and again, using people as tools. In his flight from Absalom he does the reverse: he releases Ittai, the priests and Hushai, giving each a choice (2 Samuel 15:19–37). The king who learned power on the roof learns humility on the Mount of Olives.

sections.b: Bathsheba is introduced through the men in her life: "Eliam's daughter, the wife of Uriah the Hittite" (2 Samuel 11:3). Her father and husband were both among David's elite soldiers, and her grandfather may have been Ahithophel (2 Samuel 23:34). David sees her bathing, sends for her, and lies with her; her only recorded words are "I'm pregnant" (2 Samuel 11:5). After Uriah's death she mourns him and becomes David's wife. Nathan's parable pictures her as a poor man's ewe lamb, "like a daughter" (2 Samuel 12:3), a word that echoes her name. Her first son dies; her second is Solomon, whom the LORD loves (2 Samuel 12:24). Readers debate her part: some see a willing partner or a shrewd political figure (Randall Bailey), many see a victim of royal power (Richard Davidson, Cheryl Exum), and literary critics point out that the narrator deliberately leaves her thoughts untold (Meir Sternberg, Gale Yee). Her voice is heard fully only later, as Solomon's mother (1 Kings 1–2).
sections.refs: 2 Samuel 11:2–5; 2 Samuel 11:26–27; 2 Samuel 12:1–4; 2 Samuel 12:15–25; 2 Samuel 23:34; 1 Kings 1:11–31

common: Bathsheba is often remembered as a temptress, though the text never says she sought David's attention.
uncommon: Some modern scholars, notably Randall Bailey, think Bathsheba's family, linked to Ahithophel, made the marriage politically useful to David, and many modern commentators suggest that Ahithophel's support for Absalom was revenge.

sections.h: Bathsheba and Tamar in David's house
sections.b: Two stories in the court history of David involve a king's power over a woman's body. David "sent messengers and took" Bathsheba (2 Samuel 11:4); whether she could have refused a king is the center of the modern debate, and Nathan's parable places the whole guilt on the man (2 Samuel 12:1–9). In 2 Samuel 13, Amnon tricks his half-sister Tamar into his room and rapes her. Her protest uses the words of Dinah's story: "Do not dishonor me. Such a thing is not done in Israel. Do not do this disgraceful thing" (2 Samuel 13:12; Genesis 34:7; Judges 19:23). The narrator stresses force: "He overpowered her, dishonored her and lay with her" (2 Samuel 13:14). Afterward Amnon hates her and throws her out, which she calls a greater wrong, since the law would have required him to marry her (Deuteronomy 22:28–29). Tamar's public mourning, ashes and torn robe, declares her innocence. David is angry but does nothing (2 Samuel 13:21), and her brother's revenge leads to murder and civil war.
sections.refs: 2 Samuel 11:2–5; 2 Samuel 12:1–9; 2 Samuel 13:1–22; Genesis 34:2–7; Judges 19:23; Deuteronomy 22:28–29

uncommon: Some readers argue that the narrator presents Bathsheba's story and Tamar's as deliberate mirrors, so that David's failure to judge Amnon is shown to grow out of his own sin.

sections.b: Amnon, David's firstborn, "loved" his beautiful half-sister Tamar, Absalom's full sister. Advised by his cousin Jonadab, he pretended to be sick and asked David to send Tamar to make him food. Alone with her, he seized her. Tamar pleaded, naming the act a "disgraceful thing" and offering a lawful way: "just speak to the king. He will not hold me back from you" (2 Samuel 13:13). He raped her, then hated her more than he had loved her, and had her thrown out. She tore her long royal robe, the same kind of robe Joseph wore (Genesis 37:3), and went away crying aloud. Absalom told her to be silent and took her into his house, "a woman left desolate" (2 Samuel 13:20). David was furious but did nothing, according to the longer text because he loved Amnon, his firstborn. Two years later Absalom had Amnon killed at a sheep-shearing feast (2 Samuel 13:23–29).
sections.refs: 2 Samuel 13:1–39; Genesis 37:3; Leviticus 18:9; Deuteronomy 22:28–29; Mishnah Avot 5:16

common: Amnon's love turning to hate (2 Samuel 13:15) is often cited as a picture of lust, which seeks to take, not to give.
uncommon: The Talmud holds that Tamar was the daughter of a captive woman and so not legally Amnon's sister, which is why she could suggest marriage (Sanhedrin 21a).

sections.h: Absalom from exile to the oak
sections.b: Absalom, David's third son, avenged his sister Tamar by killing Amnon and fled to his grandfather in Geshur (2 Samuel 13:37–38). Joab used a wise woman from Tekoa to persuade David to bring him back, but David kept him from court for two years (2 Samuel 14). Handsome and admired, Absalom won the people by sitting at the gate and promising justice: he "stole the hearts of the men of Israel" (2 Samuel 15:6). He had himself proclaimed king in Hebron, drove David from Jerusalem, and on Ahithophel's advice took David's concubines publicly (2 Samuel 15–16). Persuaded by Hushai to wait, he lost the battle in the forest of Ephraim; caught by the head in an oak, he was killed by Joab against David's orders and buried under a heap of stones (2 Samuel 18:9–17). David's lament for him, "My son Absalom! My son, my son Absalom!" (2 Samuel 18:33), is one of the most famous cries of grief in literature.

common: Absalom was hanged by his long hair; the text says his head caught in the oak, and the hair detail comes from later tradition (Mishnah Sotah 1:8).
uncommon: Some historians think Absalom's revolt drew on real grievances among the northern tribes and in Hebron, not only on Absalom's charm.

claude.title: Claude's reading: peace in his name
claude.body: My own observation: Absalom's name means "my father is peace" (shalom). The chapter of his death turns on the word: Ahimaaz shouts "Peace!" and David asks twice, "Is it peace for the young man?" (2 Samuel 18:28–32). The son named for his father's peace is the one for whom there is none.

sections.b: Ahithophel of Giloh was David's adviser, whose advice was regarded "as if someone had asked for a word from God" (2 Samuel 16:23). He joined Absalom at Hebron (2 Samuel 15:12), and David's one-line prayer was, "LORD, please make Ahithophel's advice foolish" (2 Samuel 15:31). He advised Absalom to take his father's concubines publicly, making the break final (2 Samuel 16:21–22), and to strike David that same night with twelve thousand men (2 Samuel 17:1–3). When Absalom chose Hushai's plan instead, Ahithophel went home, set his affairs in order and hanged himself (2 Samuel 17:23). If his son Eliam was Bathsheba's father (2 Samuel 11:3; 2 Samuel 23:34), he was Bathsheba's grandfather, and many modern commentators suggest he turned against David out of revenge, though the Talmud gives his motive as ambition (Sanhedrin 101b). Christian readers have long seen him as a type of Judas, through Psalm 41:9 and Psalm 55:12–14.
sections.refs: 2 Samuel 15:12; 2 Samuel 15:31; 2 Samuel 16:20–23; 2 Samuel 17:1–23; 2 Samuel 23:34; Psalm 41:9; Matthew 27:5

uncommon: The Mishnah counts Ahithophel among the few Israelites who have no share in the world to come (Mishnah Sanhedrin 10:2).

sections.b: The LORD sends Nathan to David after Uriah's death (2 Samuel 12:1). Instead of accusing the king directly, Nathan tells a case for judgment: a rich man who stole a poor man's only lamb. David condemns the man, and Nathan answers, "You are the man!" (2 Samuel 12:7). He reminds David of all God gave him, names his crimes against Uriah, and announces that the sword will not leave his house and that his wives will be taken in public (2 Samuel 12:7–12). When David confesses, Nathan declares that the LORD has put away his sin, but the child will die (2 Samuel 12:13–14). After Solomon's birth Nathan brings the name Jedidiah, "beloved of the LORD" (2 Samuel 12:25). The scene has become a classic picture of a prophet speaking truth to power.

sections.h: Joab in the years of Absalom
sections.b: Joab carries out David's letter ordering Uriah's death and sends back a coded report (2 Samuel 11:14–25). He captures Rabbah's water city and calls David to take the credit (2 Samuel 12:26–28). He arranges Absalom's return through the wise woman of Tekoa (2 Samuel 14:1–23), but stays away until Absalom burns his field (2 Samuel 14:29–33). In the battle against Absalom he commands a third of the army, and when he hears Absalom is hanging in an oak, he drives three sticks into his heart against the king's public order (2 Samuel 18:14). An unnamed soldier who refused to do it tells Joab plainly that Joab would have abandoned him (2 Samuel 18:12–13). Readers still debate whether Joab saved the kingdom or simply removed a rival.

When Nathan says "You are the man!", David answers with two Hebrew words, chata'ti laYHWH, "I have sinned against the LORD" (2 Samuel 12:13). Unlike Saul, who said "I have sinned" and then explained himself and asked for honor (1 Samuel 15:24–30), David offers no excuse. Nathan replies that the LORD has put away his sin. The heading of Psalm 51 ties that psalm to this moment, and Jews and Christians alike have used it as the classic prayer of repentance: "A heart broken and crushed, O God, you will not look down on" (Psalm 51:17). Repentance here brings forgiveness but not the removal of every consequence: the child dies, and David accepts it, saying "I am the one who will go to him" (2 Samuel 12:23). The Talmud teaches that David's sin was recorded so that anyone who sins would know the way back is open (Avodah Zarah 4b–5a).

sections.h: A king under law, and a king's son who wanted the throne
sections.b: 2 Samuel 11–18 tests kingship from two sides. David, the anointed king, takes another man's wife and has him killed, and a prophet tells him to his face that he is guilty (2 Samuel 12:7–9): the king is under God's law, as Deuteronomy 17:18–20 required. Absalom shows the dangers of kingship sought for its own sake: he takes a chariot and fifty runners, the very signs Samuel warned about (1 Samuel 8:11; 2 Samuel 15:1), wins the people with promises of justice (2 Samuel 15:2–6), has himself proclaimed king with the ram's horn (2 Samuel 15:10), and claims the throne by taking his father's concubines (2 Samuel 16:21–22). David, by contrast, leaves the ark in Jerusalem and his fate in God's hands (2 Samuel 15:25–26).
sections.refs: 2 Samuel 12:7–9; 2 Samuel 15:1–12; 2 Samuel 15:25–26; 2 Samuel 16:21–22; Deuteronomy 17:14–20; 1 Samuel 8:11–18

sections.b: Two psalm headings point into 2 Samuel 11–18. Psalm 51 is "a psalm of David, when Nathan the prophet came to him, after David had come to Bathsheba" (Psalm 51:0), and is read as David's prayer after 2 Samuel 12:13. Psalm 3 is "a psalm of David, when he ran away from his son Absalom" (Psalm 3:0), set in his flight over the Mount of Olives (2 Samuel 15:30). Psalm 63, "when he was in the wilderness of Judah," may also belong to the flight. Brevard Childs argued that these headings were added by later scribes who read the psalms alongside the stories, inviting readers to hear David's inner life behind the narrative's reticence. Many traditional readers hold that the headings record the real occasions.

2 Samuel has two of the Old Testament's clearest "juridical parables": made-up legal cases brought to a king so that he will pass judgment and then discover he has judged himself. Nathan's story of the rich man and the poor man's ewe lamb (2 Samuel 12:1–7) exposes David's sin. The wise woman of Tekoa's story of two brothers (2 Samuel 14:4–20), written by Joab, leads David to bring Absalom home. Uriel Simon, who named the form, also counted 1 Kings 20:35–43 and Isaiah 5:1–7. The form works only if the hearer does not recognize himself in the story until it is too late.

sections.h: God hidden in the court of David
sections.b: In 2 Samuel 11–18 God rarely acts openly: no miracles, few prophetic words, no angels. Yet three short sentences reveal his hand: the LORD's displeasure at David's sin (2 Samuel 11:27), the LORD's love for Solomon (2 Samuel 12:24), and the explanation of Absalom's choice: "The LORD had given orders to undo Ahithophel's good advice, so that the LORD could bring ruin on Absalom" (2 Samuel 17:14). David's prayer that Ahithophel's advice be made foolish (2 Samuel 15:31) is answered through Hushai's loyalty and rhetoric. Gerhard von Rad saw this hidden providence as the theology of the whole court history: God works through human choices, even sinful ones, without overriding them.
sections.refs: 2 Samuel 11:27; 2 Samuel 12:24; 2 Samuel 15:31–34; 2 Samuel 16:10–12; 2 Samuel 17:14; Genesis 50:20

sections.b: When Absalom rejects his advice, Ahithophel saddles his donkey, goes home, gives orders for his household, and hangs himself (2 Samuel 17:23). He is buried in his father's tomb, which suggests that his death brought no public dishonor on his body. Readers usually explain the act as foresight: he knew Absalom would now lose and that he, the chief traitor, would be executed. Christian readers have long paired him with Judas (Matthew 27:5), another trusted friend who betrayed his master and then hanged himself.

Absalom's head caught in the branches of a great oak, and he was left hanging "between the sky and the ground" while his mule went on (2 Samuel 18:9). Joab killed him there, and he was buried under a heap of stones (2 Samuel 18:14–17), the burial given to Achan and to the king of Ai, who was hanged on a tree (Joshua 7:26; Joshua 8:29). Readers have long connected the scene with the law that "a man who is hanged is cursed by God" (Deuteronomy 21:23), which Paul applies to Christ (Galatians 3:13).

David leaves ten concubines to keep the palace when he flees (2 Samuel 15:16). On Ahithophel's advice Absalom goes in to them in a tent on the palace roof, "with all Israel watching" (2 Samuel 16:22), fulfilling Nathan's word (2 Samuel 12:11) and claiming the throne. When David returns he keeps them shut away, provided for but never again his wives (2 Samuel 20:3). Taking a king's women was a claim to his throne, as Abner, Absalom and Adonijah all show (2 Samuel 3:7; 1 Kings 2:13–25).
sections.refs: 2 Samuel 12:8; 2 Samuel 12:11; 2 Samuel 15:16; 2 Samuel 16:21–22; 2 Samuel 20:3; 1 Kings 2:13–25

sections.b: As David flees Jerusalem, Ziba, the steward of Mephibosheth's lands, meets him with donkeys, bread, fruit and wine, and claims that Mephibosheth stayed behind hoping that "the house of Israel will hand my father's kingdom back to me" (2 Samuel 16:3). David at once gives Ziba all of Mephibosheth's property (2 Samuel 16:4). When David returns, Mephibosheth tells a different story (2 Samuel 19:24–30). Most readers think Ziba lied; the narrator lets the reader decide.

Absalom, born in Hebron (2 Samuel 3:2–3), asks leave to go there to pay a vow he says he made in exile, and there he has himself proclaimed king, with a signal of ram's horns carried through all the tribes (2 Samuel 15:7–12). The choice of David's first capital may have played on resentment in Judah's old center after the court moved to Jerusalem, and on the memory that David himself had first been made king there (2 Samuel 2:4; 2 Samuel 5:3). Two hundred guests from Jerusalem went with Absalom without knowing the plan, which made them look like supporters.

David's lament for Absalom is not a composed song like his laments for Saul and Jonathan or for Abner, but a broken cry: "My son Absalom! My son, my son Absalom! Oh, if only I had died in your place, I myself! Absalom, my son, my son!" (2 Samuel 18:33). He repeats "my son" five times in one verse. The Talmud says that his eight cries of "my son" (with 2 Samuel 19:4) lifted Absalom out of Gehinnom (Sotah 10b). The cry inspired Renaissance motets and William Faulkner's novel Absalom, Absalom!

sections.h: Loyal foreigners in David's darkest days
sections.b: Some of the most loyal people in 2 Samuel 11–18 are foreigners. Uriah the Hittite refuses to go home while the ark and the army are in the field (2 Samuel 11:11). Ittai the Gittite, a Philistine refugee who had arrived only "yesterday," swears to follow David "for death or for life" (2 Samuel 15:19–21), in words that echo Ruth's pledge to Naomi (Ruth 1:16–17). David's bodyguard of Kerethites and Pelethites stays with him (2 Samuel 15:18). A Cushite carries the true news of Absalom's death (2 Samuel 18:21–32), and Shobi, an Ammonite prince, feeds David's army (2 Samuel 17:27).

Uriah reminds David that "the ark, Israel and Judah are living in shelters" at the siege of Rabbah (2 Samuel 11:11). When David flees Absalom, Zadok and the Levites bring the ark out of the city, but David sends it back: "If the LORD looks on me with favor, he will bring me back" (2 Samuel 15:25). Unlike Israel at Aphek, which carried the ark into battle as a guarantee of victory (1 Samuel 4:3–11), David will not use God's presence as a tool.

sections.h: The blood avenger in the Tekoa story
sections.b: The wise woman of Tekoa's invented case turns on the blood avenger (go'el haddam): her surviving son killed his brother, and the clan demands his death (2 Samuel 14:6–7, 11). The law allowed this for murder (Numbers 35:19–21) and provided cities of refuge only for accidental killing. The woman asks the king to override the custom to save her family's name, and he swears to protect the son. She then applies the case to Absalom, who had killed his brother Amnon.

sections.h: A God who brings the banished home
sections.b: The wise woman of Tekoa tells David, "God does not take a life away; he works out plans so the banished one is not cast away from him" (2 Samuel 14:14). Jewish and Christian readers have heard in these words one of the Old Testament's most striking statements of God's mercy toward sinners and exiles. In context they are a plea that the king imitate God, though David's own mercy toward Absalom remains half-hearted (2 Samuel 14:24).

Absalom builds his revolt on a claim that the king does not give justice: he stands by the gate, tells every man his case is "good and straight," and says, "Oh, if someone would make me judge in the land!" (2 Samuel 15:2–4). Whether there were real grievances or only clever flattery, the story shows how a ruler's failure to hear the people's cases, or a rival's claim that he has failed, can unravel a kingdom. David's own failure to act on Tamar's rape (2 Samuel 13:21) lies in the background.

sections.h: "I am the one who will go to him"
sections.b: When his infant son dies, David stops fasting and says, "I am the one who will go to him. He will not come back to me" (2 Samuel 12:23). Many read this as David's expectation that he too will go down to the grave or Sheol, the place of the dead. Many Christians hear in it a hope of reunion after death, and the verse is often used to comfort parents who lose young children.

The war with Ammon frames the Bathsheba story. Joab besieges Rabbah while David stays in Jerusalem (2 Samuel 11:1), Uriah dies near its wall (2 Samuel 11:17), and after Joab takes the water city, David captures the citadel, takes the heavy gold crown of "their king," perhaps the god Milcom, and puts the people to forced labor (2 Samuel 12:26–31). Later Shobi son of Nahash, an Ammonite prince, brings supplies to David in his flight (2 Samuel 17:27).

The story of Tamar deliberately echoes Dinah's. Shechem "took her and lay with her and dishonored her" (Genesis 34:2), and Jacob's sons called it "a disgraceful thing in Israel" (Genesis 34:7). Amnon "overpowered her, dishonored her and lay with her" (2 Samuel 13:14), and Tamar called it a "disgraceful thing" (2 Samuel 13:12). In both stories the father hears and does nothing, and the victim's full brother takes bloody revenge (Genesis 34:25–26; 2 Samuel 13:28–29).

sections.h: Loyal love in the flight from Absalom
sections.b: David blesses Ittai with "loyal love and faithfulness" (2 Samuel 15:20), and Ittai answers by showing exactly that loyalty. Absalom mocks Hushai, "Is this your loyal love for your friend?" (2 Samuel 16:17), not knowing that Hushai is staying behind out of loyal love for David. Hesed in these chapters is the loyalty of friends and servants in a time of betrayal.

sections.h: David on the Mount of Olives
sections.b: Christian readers since the church fathers have seen David's flight from Absalom as a foreshadowing of Jesus' passion: the rejected king crosses the Kidron (2 Samuel 15:23; John 18:1), climbs the Mount of Olives weeping (2 Samuel 15:30; Luke 19:41; Luke 22:39), and is betrayed by a trusted counselor who later hangs himself (2 Samuel 17:23; Matthew 27:5), a link made through Psalm 41:9 and John 13:18. Jewish readers see in the same scene David's humility under God's discipline.
